utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. Before we start the examination of the first witness, we have to deal with a few things, and I would like to do it as quickly as possible. First of all, Madam Registrar, I think still decisions have been taken on the exhibits that were tendered in respect of Witness DP3.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1756 under seal, pseudonym sheet; Exhibit P3751 under seal, application for pension in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The documents are admitted into evidence. We will deal with the DP51 exhibits not at this very moment because this witness still has to return. Then I have a few issues that I would like to bring to the attention of the parties. Although a written decision, a more general one, on the protective measures sought will be given, the Chamber would like to receive by next Friday further details with respect to further witnesses that will be called this month so we have already the information available and that we don't have to wait until the arrival of the witnesses. And as the Defence is aware of -- especially details in respect of the proceedings pending for the return of property might be of importance. And the Chamber would also like very much to be informed about what is most important for the witnesses in respect of the pseudonym on the one hand side which would cause them to remain unknown to the local authorities, or safe conduct on the other hand that would create the need to inform the local authorities of the identity of these witnesses. So we would like to be informed about that by next Friday for the witnesses still to be called this month and one week later for all the remaining witnesses. Then we also have one of the witnesses for which a videolink was asked for. The request was based on surgery this witness had to undergo or has undergone. This Chamber would very much like to be informed in more detail about the type of surgery, time for recovery, et cetera. Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was hearing something on my -- I think I was tuned into the French channel. If I may ask, Mr. President, Your Honours, in respect to the further details that the Defence provides a date of birth and father's name of each witness. The difficulty which it presents is also sometimes when we try to do our research, we come up with material for persons. And it could save the court some time, primarily asking witnesses about matters which are not relevant to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please give the personal data in such a way that the persons can be identified. I think date of birth and name of the father would be good criteria. Then I think -- yes, please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Mr. President, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we will take a lot of time, otherwise I will ask the usher to get the witness into the courtroom unless it is an issue that you would like to discuss or to bring to our attention in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, the laptop problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Same is true for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the same is true for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There is one button that says "disconnect," but if it's not connected yet. This happens almost every time now, every day. So I do understand that there is some search for better solutions than to repair every day the shortcomings. Could we be assisted today, and I hope we will not be confronted with it for the next 70 days. Then, Mr. Usher, could you please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I -- Mr. Stamp, it is always difficult to chose between you and the Registrar, but if you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't understand the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, both important people in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect -- I am so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I thought you understood what my choice would be, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I do beg your pardon. In respect of the witness DP1, we had indicated that as soon as available, we would provide coloured copies of the black and white exhibits that were used. In the testimony, the exhibit number is P3750, and we have now coloured copies which we would like to tender up to the Court through the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I take it that you are Mr. Konstantin Kacalin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you in Russian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. I will read that solemn declaration to you. It will then be translated for you into Russian. Would you then please repeat it. I will do it in small parts. I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I declare that I shall speak the truth, nothing but the truth, and only the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The translation was not the usual following order. May I take it that when you solemnly declared that you would speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, that is what you declared in Russian? Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask the witness and the parties especially to take care that no one speaks before the previous phrases have been translated. Because we have Russian translated, but it is two translators who cannot overlap each other. So, therefore, I must ask you, Mr. Kacalin, not to speak until everything has been translated, and you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, not to put a next question to the witness until the moment that everything is translated. Then finally, I was informed that the translation services that had been applied for rather late are available today and not tomorrow anymore, both the technical and the persons involved. So I may urge the parties to see that they will finish, if possible, the examination of this witness today. So make it as efficient as possible. Ms. Pilipovic, is it you or is it Mr. Piletta-Zanin who will examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the microphone it is better. Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, witness. Can you hear me? Can you hear me all right?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: This is not quite what the witness said, but it is not serious. Witness, will you please tell us first: What are your professional qualifications, that is, can you tell us something about your professional training in just so many words.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I graduated from the university in Moscow, majoring in journalism. I have been a journalist for 30 years in the state radio and television in the U.S.S.R., the broadcasting service for Yugoslavia because I speak Serbo-Croat. After that, I worked for the Mayak Radio station for a rather long time. And I was also a former correspondent of the Mayak Radio station from the Balkans stationed in Zagreb, Sarajevo and Ljubljana. I went to the Balkans, and lately I have been working in a television service, the so-called third federal channel as editor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. When you say that you were correspondent do you by this mean a war correspondent? You can answer by yes or no, and I would be grateful if you do.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you cover the developments related to Sarajevo? If yes, when?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes, among other things, from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My question was also, Witness, if yes, then when? I do not have the Russian channel. I do not know whether that was interpreted, but when was that?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I worked in Sarajevo from 1995 to 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I wasn't really listening, but I see that you worked in Sarajevo in 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes. I worked in that period permanently in that period from Sarajevo and from Zagreb, but I travelled to these places even before in 1993, and 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us when you travelled there in 1994, what occasion did -- and at what time of the year where you in Sarajevo that year. On the transcript I said 1993, 9-3, not 9-4.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes, it was in 1993. A group of journalists, including myself; there were several people in the group. There was also Aleksandar Kaverniev, correspondent from the Komsomolskaja Pravda; another person from Moscow, Novoe Novosti [phoen]; Mrs. Irena Lagunina from Novoe Vreme. We were together in Sarajevo from July 1993 for about a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, were you officially invited to go? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes, I was officially invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, who was it that formally and officially invited you to visit Sarajevo in 1993?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: It was a representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Moscow. He called himself ambassador. I don't remember his last name now. But he is still working in the Foreign Ministry of Bosnia. We can find that out. He is in charge of Russian affairs. It was him who invited a group of journalists from Moscow from very well-known publications Inasha [phoen] as well as television and press journalists including radio journalists. At the time, I was radio journalist. They invited us to visit Sarajevo, and the Bosnian side took it upon themselves to organise everything and make all the arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I would like you to tell me: Did you meet with officials -- with public figures in Sarajevo, and will you tell me yes or no. Thank you. I will come back to that later. I am still talking about 1993, 9-3, did you then have an opportunity to visit the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am not sure of the answer to the previous question is recorded on the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I make the same observation. I think the answer of the witness was that he did meet officials, public figures, and that then the next question of Mr. Piletta-Zanin was whether the witness had any opportunity to visit the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was correct, Mr. President. Thank you. Perhaps the first one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...repeat it, because it was translated in French, so I take it that the witness has answered that first question. And, therefore, we would like to hear the answer to the second question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So, Witness, were you able to during that stay -- and I am talking about 1993, that is 9-3 -- were you able to pay a visit to Sarajevo? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your answer was "yes," Witness. Can you briefly tell us which areas of Sarajevo were you able to visit.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: We flew into Sarajevo and landed on the Butmir airfield. Regrettably, none of the hosts met us there. And there was a Ukrainian officer instead who came to the airport and took us to the town in an APC. We were driving in this APC through town, and since hospitals were open, we were able to see just before the entrance into Sarajevo some devastation, destroyed buildings. And then we saw the building belonging to the Oslobodjenje newspaper. We also passed by residential buildings, and then we finally arrived at the Holiday Inn Hotel. We were unimpressed by the destruction of the Unis building and other buildings in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will stop you now. I am stopping you, Witness. I shall come back to what you have told us about your impressions, but were you able to visit what at times is called Stari Grad, that is, the Old Town, the old historic part of Sarajevo? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes, I have visited it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am now coming back to what you have just told us. Where did you stay, Witness, during your sojourn there?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I stayed in the hotel Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to know with regard to the Holiday Inn, did you have electricity? Did you get water normally, that is, was the water running in your rooms? That is, could you -- did you have access to all -- to things that usually are called urban utilities?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Maybe this question sounds strange but were you getting poor, cold meals or were you having your meals normally, that is, whether you were getting hot food and meals which were up to the standard of that hotel?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes to what?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: We had normal warm breakfasts with normal, generally accepted and Balkan meals, we had bread, butter, jam, coffee. We had our lunches regular. We had soup, we had the main course, and of course there was no great versatility, but at the same time we had normal meals, and the same I can say about dinners.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you to slow down a little bit because it is still difficult for the interpreters to follow you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not going very fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I am going to proceed about the devastation that you mentioned. When you are talking about the devastation, could you perhaps locate this geographically, if this is the case, in such-and-such a place in Sarajevo? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Seeing that you have given us an affirmative answer, could you tell us in general, Witness, what were the areas, the places, where this devastation had taken place essentially, generally?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Well, in general, I have already mentioned it was that segment of the road which was passed from the airport to the intersection where you enter the city. We -- there I observed a lot of ruins; some houses had no roofs, and some houses were comprised of just walls. And then on the right side of you go from the airport, I could observe the building Oslobodjenje, which I already mentioned, and two buildings of Unis next to the hotel Holiday Inn. And that was quite impressive and that was a sad impression, I should say, and also the building of the former -- the former building of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It used to be a huge skyscraper, and I could see it was ruined. And also we saw the hotel Europa from the centre of the city and there I could see only walls remaining from that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when you are telling us about the areas that you crossed to get to the centre, do you know if these areas, these neighbourhoods, were located on or in the vicinity of the front line?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Well, I think that if we take, for example, the building of Unis and the former building of the government, I think they were close to the line of front. And if we consider the buildings near the airport, those buildings, then I would say that, as far as I understand, they were far from the line of the front. Maybe I am wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But, Witness, do you know or don't you: At the time, where was the front line or the front lines? Did you know that at that time?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: No. We were told that the front line was on the other side. If you go towards the centre, then on the right side behind the river -- if we can it the centre of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The river, what river? Could you please specify it.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Which -- which there was the attempt on Ferdinad [phoen] and I don't remember the exact title. It was a bridge. The bridge which separates Sarajevo into two parts, that is the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I would now like us to focus in a position to the ferry, perhaps if we could focus on the centre, you visited these areas. And did you go on several occasions in these neighbourhoods in the centre, in the Old Town, Stari Grad, and so on?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Well, we were taken into several areas and to the centre, for example, we were also in the area and close to the stadium where the Olympic Games used to be held. And we also visited once the central clinical hospital of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The central hospital of Sarajevo. Does it have a name?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Well, we were told that this is the central hospital of the city located somewhere in Kosevo. I am not sure, but maybe I am wrong, but this is as far as I believe what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. We will come back later to the hospital. I would like us to focus on the centre now. In the city of Sarajevo did you see -- and I am not talking about governmental or presidential buildings or other buildings of this nature. I am talking about buildings, residential buildings. Did you see important devastation there? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: If you didn't see considerable devastation during your stay in Sarajevo, did you hear in this central Sarajevo, did you hear with your own ears a noise of explosions of shells, shell exploding in the city centre, not in the suburbs?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: No, I did not hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In this period, Witness, did you hear a specific noise of what we call the PATs, of what we call the anti-tank cannons firing in the city?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think before the witness would be able to answer that, a proper question, we should perhaps inquire whether the witness knows what the subject of the matter is, which is a PAT, an anti-tank cannon, if he knows that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think the first proper question would be whether the witness could differentiate between the sound of the -- yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, gladly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I apologise. This is my fault. I should have started with this question: Are you able with your experience, to tell apart with your ear the noise of, for instance, a tank firing, of a heavy machine-gun, or an anti-aircraft cannon? Is it possible? Could you distinguish that?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: [No translation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, to convince everyone, how is it possible to distinguish that, although there is no interpretation, I am told, and the answer was "yes."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please make longer pauses before asking a question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are being asked to make longer pauses during your interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, in order to clarify this, Witness, could you please tell us: How is it possible to distinguish a cannon fire -- cannon firing, a heavy machine-gun, or an anti-aircraft cannon with your ear?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Well first of all, as far as I know, a tank has a fairly large shell, it uses a fairly large shell, and therefore the noises that it produces is quite heavy. So one can usually distinguish this in an audio sense quite easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think I invited you to put the question to the witness not whether it was possible, but whether the witness could do that. Because your question was about specific noises he could identify. Can you make such distinctions between the different weaponry being fired? Because your answer included "as far as." Can you do that yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, Witness, during your stay in 1993, did you hear, first of all, cannon firing on the city; then secondly, heavy machine-gun firing on the city; and three, anti-aircraft cannon firing on the city? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us earlier, I believe you said that you speak Serbian. Can you confirm this, please.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You speak Serbian?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I speak Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have the possibility of speaking directly without an interpreter with the inhabitants of Sarajevo at the time?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were you able to -- or what did you talk about with these people, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: We talked them -- we, as journalists, asked people how they lived in Sarajevo. We also asked them about what was going on, why did the war break out. We asked the people how was life for them and whether they lacked something, and we usually got typical answers from people, regardless of their ethnic origin. They said they didn't -- they usually said that they didn't have water, electricity, natural gas, and so on, but that they had this very natural desire to fight, to preserve, normal living conditions in their town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. If you were to describe the state of mind, how would you do that? What words would you use to tell us how the people in Sarajevo felt at the time according to your own experience and according to your personal contacts that you had?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I could say that those people were quite depressed by what was going on in the town and all the things that they lack; however, they had a very strong surviving spirit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were you told, for instance, if -- that -- if people were committing suicides more frequently? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice that, but I learned about it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In respect of the people in Sarajevo as well, did you see, during your stay, wounded or perhaps people who were killed not in hospitals, but in the streets of Sarajevo? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Not on the streets, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you would not mind, I would like to ask one question to the witness, since he just told us that you were not told that people were committing suicides more frequently, but that you didn't notice that at that time, but you learned about it later on. But what did you learn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later on, when I came back to Sarajevo, I had a conversation with my colleagues, and I received quite a lot of information from western sources, and was told that there were quite frequent suicide cases in Sarajevo. But while I was there, while I was in Sarajevo, there was no talk of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if we can please come back to the streets of Sarajevo. Was it possible for you to see - and believe it was - to see people and there were people who were civilians and people who were soldiers during your visit of Sarajevo neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: People in uniforms and with weapons were military, and people in civilian clothes were civilians. There were both kinds of people in the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you are telling us about people in uniform in Sarajevo, and since you tell us that they were armed, could you tell us what type of weapons did they carry?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is difficult for me to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps an objection is a little bit too late --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please use your microphone in such a way that I can better hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am sorry. Perhaps the objection might be a little bit too late because counsel has already -- or what appears to be of a leading question. But it might have been the transcript. Can I be directed, if counsel would assist me, as to the part of the transcript where the witness said that he saw persons who were armed. I have it here in one of the questions counsel said, "and since you tell us that they were armed." I am afraid I did not see that part in my transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, do I in on page 16 and line 10, "people with uniforms and with weapons." That is what I understood to be armed of the next question of Mr. Piletta-Zanin. So he inquired what weapons, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. I think it was an unnecessary interruption, Mr. Stamp, but please take care of that. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asking what weapons the witness then saw the people wearing. Please answer that question, Mr. Kacalin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I am not sure that I heard the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us what was your answer to the question, the legitimate question that I asked before I was interrupted: What type of weapons were these people carrying? Can I help you perhaps, were they large weapons or were they personal weapons and so on?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I saw people with pistols. They used to call them T-T pistols, Yugoslav make. People used to show those pistols to me. And I also saw automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us, what type of automatic rifle, if you can.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: It was generally a Kalashnikov automatic rifle, well-known in the whole world.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: AK-47 type?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't distinguish the 47. It was a Kalashnikov, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, to the best of your recollection, all the soldiers that you were able to see in the city, were they all armed?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Well it is difficult to claim now whether all of them -- not all of them had them. But I talked to officers of the Bosnian army and the general from that army, and there were armed people there. In the place where I lived, there were members of the Bosnian army and they were armed and I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These people that you saw still in the city of Sarajevo, were they visible in small quantities, one soldier here, one over there, or were they in small groups or in perhaps larger groups? What can you tell us on this subject please.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember whether I saw groups. But I did meet soldiers. I couldn't tell you whether they were privates or officers, senior or junior officers. But it is true that we saw armed people in town and that we saw a lot of them in the barracks, yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. These soldiers, how were they moving about, on foot, or perhaps did you see that this was the case, using other means of transport?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: They were mostly walking. The soldiers were on foot, but we didn't walk about the city that often so as to believe able to see a large number of armed people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you were, however, able to see, I believe, several neighbourhoods in the city. Is that correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to see that this city had a number of cultural and/or religious monuments?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: We visited the mosque, the central mosque which has been remodelled lately; it was just slightly damaged. We entered the mosque and we saw the praying of people there. We also went to the Catholic church. We met with the Catholic cardinal of Sarajevo, and we also met with the chief mufti [phoen] of Sarjevo, Mr. Ceric, if I remember him correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, telling us about the mosque, were you able to see with your own eyes possible -- and I am stressing this word -- possible examples of mosques that were destroyed, that is, shelled and so on? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: No, most likely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you were in Sarajevo, were minarets damaged as such, generally speaking, or in a considerable way, to a considerable degree?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: There was partial damage. I just can't remember right now, but as far as the central mosque is concerned, everything was in order there. There were just traces of shells or bullets. Yes, that's true. But it was difficult to say how many minarets were damaged because there is such a large number of minarets in Sarajevo, a huge number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you yourself know about one single minaret that was destroyed in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. I am going to come back to the destruction of buildings. Do you know, Witness, what was occasionally in Sarajevo called a pavement rose?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes. I saw such traces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you perhaps confirm if this is the case, what, in your opinion, is a "pavement rose," so that we know that we are talking about the same thing.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Well, when there is a depression in the pavement and if they are there -- I don't know how to call them properly. Whether branches of a rose and they are going in a different direction. There is simply a depression and shrapnel traces in the pavement in different directions. So one can tell that this is where the shell landed in the pavement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. When you were in Sarajevo in 1993 in the neighbourhoods that you visited, did you see many such pavement roses in the city? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you pay attention to the state of the buildings that were around you, that were surrounding you, particularly the roofs? In 1993, in July, how would an observer see the roofs of the neighbourhoods that you visited? And I am from this question excluding large official buildings. I am talking about normal houses in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: So excluding large buildings. Well, excluding these buildings, I already talked told to you about the road that went from the airport to Sarajevo, and there were a lot of destroyed houses there, a number of them without roofs. I didn't count how many because we passed through the road quite quickly. But there were such houses, yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, your answer that you gave me is to do with the peripheral of areas that you have to cross in order to get to the centre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. But now I am asking you a question in relation to the neighbourhoods in the centre of Sarajevo. So that is relatively far away from the combat areas, for instance, Bascarsija and others. What did they look like?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Well, it seemed to me that in the centre of town, there were no -- not that many small houses and there were no houses with roofs missing. However, if one looked from the Holiday Inn building, then one could see up there in the hills, those houses that were damaged. Yes, if looking from the hotel, one could see such buildings in the distance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could one, therefore, at the time distinguish with regard to destruction between areas called peripheral and central zone? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And Witness, according to you, this difference was reflected in what, that is, where were the areas of major destruction? Was it along the peripheral or was it in the central area?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: My worst impressions were from the peripheral areas near the airport. But in the centre of the city on large buildings, some of the window panes were shattered, some of them were hit by shells. You could see that there were strafed by bullets from machine-guns and automatic rifles. But as far as damage of the kind that prevents you from living in them, people managed. They closed holes with all sorts of materials plastic polyethylene, whatever, and continued to live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, perhaps I shall come back to this. But these are tall buildings that we are talking about, these are public buildings, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I am talking about residential buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were -- about to explain about the leading --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, the witness answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness answered, and I take it the objection doesn't stand anymore. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am now going back to the buildings. You tell us about these residential building, so why -- no, first: Where would you say those buildings are, in peripheral areas or in non-peripheral areas?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I am now talking about the places which were not far from the Holiday Inn Hotel. In fact, my impression of Sarajevo is as if it consisted of one long street leading to the centre. And the areas I am talking about was Alipasino Polje, Alipasino field, where the UN headquarters are now, and the buildings lining that street. Some of the residential buildings there that I saw were damaged. I don't know in the course of which battles, but the window panes were shattered. You could see bullet holes on them. And there were two destroyed buildings which produced most awful impression on me, the Unis company building, and one government building which is still standing. I visited Sarajevo again in the March of this year on a business trip to make story about the 10th anniversary of the Dayton Accord. So I was on mission there recently, and some of the things remain standing as I had seen them in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when you talk to us about Alipasino Polje, but saying that it is in front of the current UN building, don't you think -- and unfortunately I have to ask a leading question, Mr. President, because I have no other way of putting this question -- one would say that that was another area, an area which was called Vojnicko Polje rather?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it is my recollection that the transcript tells me that the witness did not say that Alipasino Polje was in front of the current UN building, but his testimony was that Alipasino Polje is where the UN headquarters are now. So did I understand you well that you said that the UN headquarters are in an area you know as Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not asserting it is Alipasino Polje. I am just saying that this piece of Sarajevo where the UN building is standing now and next to it, right next to it, they are building a new mosque. I am talking about the residential area there that we had seen at the time, and where we had seen damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And apart from those residential buildings, in the part which is more to the east if I am correct, that is, closer to Stari Grad after Alipasino Polje towards the centre, did you see there any other destruction which would be comparable? Yes or no. I am talking about residential buildings.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And these residential buildings, how many floors, more or less, did they have?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: 15 or 20. Those were high-rise building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know if it was possible to fire across there with some firearms, whether it be hunting rifles, snipers but through these buildings? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I think it was quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I shall rephrase my question. I was not saying "firing from these buildings," but going through the buildings, bullets going through these buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, let me first ask one question to

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question to you was whether with hunting rifles or snipers it would be possible to fire through these buildings, that is what my transcript says. And your answer was, "I think it was quite possible." Is this a misunderstanding or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it seems I misunderstood. Of course it is a misunderstanding. From a hunting rifle, it is absolutely impossible to fire in such a way as to hit the building through. Maybe from another heavier weapon that was possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would mean you understood the question as "firing through an undamaged building"? Because I take it from your answer that you are talking about firing through a building, breaking through glass, walls, whatever would be in that building. Is that correct? And you said, "That was impossible."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. My question had to do with a hunting rifle. But am I to take your answer as an answer applying to all the personal weapons, rifles, pistols, whatever? I am talking about light firearms. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like us, Witness, to move away towards the hospital that we visited, that is the Sarajevo hospital called central hospital. You told us that it was at Kosevo, and we call it the Kosevo Hospital. Was it a hospital around which there was a park? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. And were there several buildings?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you see only one or several buildings of that complex called the Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I think it was one. We were simply taken to one of the wards with patients, and we talked to the head doctor, he introduced himself as the chief neurologist surgeon who had been wounded recently and had just come back to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. So when you went into that building, was it the first, say, in the park, or the second, or the third building in that park, or I don't know? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I think we were in the central building. We were taken to the children's ward, because the ward we visited was occupied by sick children.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Was it the maternity ward, what one calls maternity ward?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: No, it was not a maternity ward. The children were around 6, 7, up to 10 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. And during your visit to that place, Witness, could you take note of the quality and the state that the building was in? In other words, was it a building which was completely destroyed or I don't know, or would you say to the contrary? What can you tell us about your impressions of the state the building was in?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Well, practically all the buildings were intact. I haven't noticed any damage. The hospital was operating normally. There were doctors there who were treating patients. The hospital was operating as in peacetime, as in normal conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And what do you mean by this? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: What I mean is that there were patients, sick people, and there were doctors. People who had asked for medical assistance and were receiving it in the form of surgery, traditional treatment, or whatever else. The same way a hospital works in any country of the world, in Moscow, here in The Hague, or anywhere else. A little better here, a little worse there, but it was a fully functioning hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were there, for instance, some things which were out of the ordinary? I don't know, operating rooms or just rooms crowded with people? Were there people in corridors, in passages, or did you see anything that would be out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you now please tell us about what you saw outside, the park around, for instance, the hospital and those buildings? Did it look damaged? Were there any damages or buildings? What could you see there? Was it ravished by whatever -- fire? What could you see there during your visit in 1993?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: No, there was nothing of the sort. I will say again that that building -- and we did not take a very close look of the workings of the hospital -- but the impression at first glance was that it was a normally functioning hospital, receiving patients, normal patients and wounded people. We visited a ward with wounded children. We did not see crammed corridors. Everybody was lying in normal hospital beds, treated by nurses and other medical personnel. They did say that they experienced shortages of medical supplies, that they had no proper facilities for blood transfusions, et cetera. But, otherwise, they were working.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Generally speaking, what state was the roof or roofs of the buildings?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: The roofs, the roofs were normal; they were not damaged. When you go into a hospital, you don't pay a particular attention to the roof. You see that the hospital is working normally, and you don't see -- you don't notice anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you notice a cemetery next to this hospital? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I am not certain. Most possibly, yes, but I am not sure because in many streets in Sarajevo at the time, there were cemeteries. We did not distinguish between Kosevo cemetery and another cemetery, but there were a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You told us, sir, that you did not hear any shells falling on the city during your stay there. I shall be more precise. Does this also apply to the night to the nighttime? My question refers to around-the-clock occurrences.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: At night when we were already back in our hotel, we heard automatic fire at a very short distance from us in the direction of the river. It was not in the -- it was not the central street that our windows were facing, but the other side. I don't know how to describe it. We heard automatic fire from that side, and we could feel that there was fighting in the street. Somebody was opening fire from automatic weapons, and I heard bursts of automatic fire a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: We are talking about rounds fired from small arms or are we talking about heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Early from light weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: During your stay there in 1993, did you meet Sarajevo politicians, and if so, whom did you meet, in the order of importance?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Well first of all, there was Mr. Alija Izetbegovic who was President of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the leader. The second one we met was Mr. Siljadzic. We also met with clergy representatives. I already spoke of Mr. Ceric, and there was also the Catholic cardinal of Sarajevo. We also met with representatives of the Jewish community, the Sefared [phoen] Jews, and that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what did you talk about at the time when you met with Mr. Izetbegovic? How and when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: This meeting was in the building of the Presidency. It is a large building which still houses the entire leadership of the Bosnian Federation. We spent a lot of time waiting outside in the street at first before coming in. It is a building with large network of hallways, many, many doors, and there were many armed people inside. But I found it natural that it had a lot of security, because after all there was the President and the Presidency. It was a rather long meeting. On our side there was I and Mr. Nekrasin [phoen]. We were the only two who were conducting this dialogue with Mr. Izetbegovic. We ask him what the war was about, why it broke out, what was going on in Bosnia, for how long Sarajevo was going to be in that condition, how the people of Sarajevo were managing, what the life was like, how Mr. Izetbegovic and his associates were maintaining contact with the outside world. He told me that there was always a possibility to leave, but they always came back because that is where they live and work, and that's part of their life. It was a rather interesting meeting because Mr. Izetbegovic is a rather interesting collocatur. He always goes in depth and talks about details. I can't remember all of it now, but I remember it lasted an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You tell us that Mr. Izetbegovic went into detail. Did he also tell you what was it that -- what was -- what were the chief afflictions of people in Sarajevo and can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: He spoke about the fact that Sarajevo has a population where many people were dying, dying from starvation, from wounds, that the town is besieged, that it was impossible to break the siege. They had a shortage of electricity, water, bread, light, that it was a city under a blockade. And he said, We will all try to lift the blockade with our own means or with the help of outsiders, but we will not leave it. Mr. Izetbegovic was basically saying the same thing that we heard from other people, from the men in the street, so to say. He spoke as the leader of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that this is hearsay, Mr. President, but perhaps it can be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you talk about electricity, in the journalistic circles, did you -- did you talk about the possibility that the politicians in Sarajevo had themselves caused these power cuts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is the hearsay nature of this, but it is a leading question about what politicians --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether something is hearsay can be deduced from the answer. The question as such, if you ask whether this witness heard something then, of course, the content of what he heard, would be hearsay, but the fact that he heard something is of course not hearsay. Please proceed and rephrase your answer -- your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you spoke to us, Witness, about the blockade, it meant in every sense outside, and inside, from the inside to the outside, do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Well, the city was closed off, so we can agree it was blockade. And the leadership of the city claimed that it was impossible to get out, impossible for them, and impossible for the population in general. And they said that huge efforts had to be made with the help of the United Nations for them to travel anywhere over Mount Igman, on airplanes, even to reach another end of the country, let alone go abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, did you ask Mr. Alija Izetbegovic about more strategic matters? For instance, how the defence was organised, how the weapons were procured, and I don't know, many other questions of this nature.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: As far as defence is concerned, I couldn't ask questions because that is not my province. But everybody, not only I, but my colleagues too were interested in knowing how Sarajevo is managing to defend itself without having their own supply of weapons and no additional resupply of ammunition. And Mr. Izetbegovic said that we have capacities for manufacturing a certain amount of shells and ammunition, and we can hold out for a while longer. That is approximately what he said. I am not going to swear on the Bible about this. But he did say something to the effect that they had the possibility of procuring weapons, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Did you ever -- Witness, you talk to us that it was possible to procure weapons, and this, I guess will be my last question before the break: Did you ever hear mention of specific operations related to the import of weapons into the city in an illegal manner?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: We didn't know about it at the time, but later on as the war went on in Sarajevo it wasn't only 1993, but also in 1994 and in 1995, and Dayton came at the end of 1995 and the accords were signed later on in Paris. So during all that time, there was a lot of talk about the fact that the Bosnians had a lot of opportunity to procure weapons from elsewhere. However, I cannot make any claims regarding that because this, again, was information from other sources. But it is very likely that it was like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, since you indicated that that was your last question before the break, I take it that this --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course. May I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom, because I would like to just briefly speak with the parties about the rest of the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have, until now spent approximately 70 minutes on the examination-in-chief, and for this afternoon, there would be remaining approximately two hours and twenty minutes. I urge the parties to see whether it would be possible to finish the examination of this witness today. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, do you have any idea on how much time you would still need to conclude the examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be shorter, as we have said, and I say that for technical reasons, all of this lasts longer. But if there are no other interruptions, than it will be shorter than I have indicated earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us how much shorter, because I would like to make a planning for this afternoon. Would you still need another 20 minutes? 30 minutes? 40 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between 20 and 30, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I then take it that we have -- let me just write down 30 minutes for the -- for the Defence. That would take altogether one hour and 40 minutes. How much time would the Prosecution need to cross-examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Certainly not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Certainly not more than that. That means that I expect the Defence to use 30 effective minutes, and then we will at least be able to conclude the examination of this witness today. We will adjourn until 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you may proceed to examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I would like us to come back to the examination. If we can proceed in the following way: Before the break, we were talking about the talks that you had with Mr. Izetbegovic. Did anyone, perhaps, ask him any questions in respect to the existence of prisons in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Such questions were not really being asked in principle, although there were certain questions about this, but not on that occasion. I don't think that we asked Mr. Alija Izetbegovic about this, even though we knew that there were prisons in Sarajevo even before that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You say that you were aware about existence of such prisons. Witness, were these prisons for Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I cannot really claim that they were prisons for Serbs only. There were Serbs in them too. But as any state, you have people who are charged with something. So there are Serbs and Muslims, all those who violated laws, so we knew about those prisons already.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. You were telling us about criminals. Didn't you ever hear if in Sarajevo there was something comparable to a gang war was going on, and if so, could you tell us more about it?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Well, once again, our colleagues journalists spoke about it and people who have lived in Sarajevo for quite a long time lived there. I believe -- I think it was the correspondent Abli Beresons [phoen], a Frenchman or perhaps he was a Belgium. I don't remember. There was many things that happened since that time. But there was talk that there wasn't only a war between Serbs and Muslims in Sarajevo, but there were also settling of accounts, as they would say in Russia, that is, when people fold within Sarajevo, that is the opposing in the Muslim part of the city, yes, there were groups which were fighting between themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, so that we can understand you well -- so that we can understand you well, when you are talking about groups that were opposed to each other, are you talking about some isolated groups, some individuals, or are you talking about some structured groups that were part of an organisation that were perhaps armed and members of the defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That question is, as the previous question is, is very, very leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, this is not only a leading question, but on an issue that, at least, the Chamber understands is of importance for the Defence. So would you please refrain from putting these leading issues, if it concerns these kind of issues. Can I ask the next question: What do you know personally about these settlement of accounts or gangs fighting against each other? Because you just told us that you heard something from a French or a Belgian who stayed there for a longer time. Could you tell us exactly what do you know by your own observation, by your own experience, and what do you know from others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I will describe you an incident when we were in the hotel and we heard gunfire at night next to the hotel. And those were automatic weapons. So we asked a colleague, Well, you have been here a long time does it happen often? Does in the vicinity of the hotel there is frequent fighting? And my colleague journalist - and I repeat, I do not know, perhaps he was a Belgian, but we spoke French, and I can speak French, and that is why I could ask him that - he said, yes, that such incidents were quite frequent, that there was people who are squaring the accounts not between Muslim and Serbs, but between Muslim themselves. So I am not saying that there was -- that was something that happened all the time, but this happened in the Muslim part of the city and I heard it with my own ears. And I also -- one could see because they were using tracing bullets, so you could see there were exchanges of fire. And also my Belgian or my French colleague confirmed it for me. So that is the only thing that I can say. I cannot say that this was a thing that lasted all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know whether these persons or groups of persons participated in, I would say, the combat between the main parties? So do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, as you know, in general, this Chamber leaves it to the parties to examine the witnesses. If, however, questions very leading come up on such issues, it might result now and then in some additional questions from the Chamber at that very moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will just also avail myself of this opportunity to call a technician because my laptop is not working again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you just told us about the existence of these tracing bullets. Did you see them yourself?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes. Because we were on the 8th floor of the hotel, but we can see it, particularly at night we could see that there was gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you saw these bullets, were you able to identify, geographically speaking, where they were coming from and where they were going to?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I am repeating: My windows did not face the main street of the Holiday Inn, but to the south, to a south street. And where the snipers had -- and it is difficult for me, besides, I didn't really try to follow these exchanges, so where the bullets were entered and where they came from. And it usually happened later, late in the evening and late. Besides we were warned that it wasn't particularly advisable to stand by the windows to try to avoid any undesirable consequences. We saw it once or twice, and after that we were not interested to follow it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But did you know if these shots were going from the city, since the bullets were tracing bullets, were you able to see?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: It was in a very small segment -- section in front of the hotel. Because the hill started right somewhere right there. And it happened there. What I can confirm is that it was in the part of the city that we lived in; it was very nearby. It wasn't the fire coming from afar, it was right next to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Witness, do you know if these clashes caused victims or civilian victims in fact? What do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I know nothing about that, anything about what went on beyond the hotel windows. Whether particular -- whether so many people were killed on a particular night, we simply did not get that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I am now going to come back to your visit in the Old Town. There, were you able to see recent traces or signs showing that attacks were committed in the city? And what I mean by "signs" is some traces, marks on the locations. Were you able to see those signs?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: In the city, many buildings had bullet marks because the aggressors were firing toward one another and bullets frequently hit buildings. So one could see bullet marks in many parts of the central city. And I saw it in many places. That is, not everywhere, but there were such marks. There was fighting, and it attested to the fact that there was a war going on in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. When you went back to Sarajevo after this first visit, could you tell us at what time was that? What year? What period of time?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: You mean when I went to Sarajevo next after 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: So years from 1995, I visited several times. At that time, I was already the correspondent from the Balkans for the Mayak Radio station, and therefore, I travelled to Sarajevo at the -- I either went there myself or with a group of journalists. So I went with a Moscow television team, a cameraman, and another reporter. We made a series of stories and sent them to Moscow so that in 1995, I visited Sarajevo on four or five occasions. Then I went to Sarajevo three or four times in 1996, except that at that time, it was so much simpler. I would think that in 1995, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. deputy foreign minister, Ilisa Gajic [phoen] was there and he conducted investigations with Alija Izetbegovic at the time, met with Siljadzic, and also gave interviews for Mayak Radio station and for our television station, which I used of course because that allowed me to meet and talk to a number of Bosnian political figures at that time too, Siljadzic and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. When you returned to Sarajevo in 1995, could you please tell us in relation to the destruction, physical destruction inside the city of Sarajevo, if there was any, if -- were there differences between the situation in July 1993 and the time when you returned some months later in 1995?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Practically nothing changed, that is this part around the airport was as destroyed. Oslobodjenje building was as destroyed. Unis skyscraper and others were still destroyed. The government building was in the same state. That is what I saw in 1993 was what I saw again in 1995, 1996, and now there is some slight change. I was in March this year, I repeat this, there, and I talked with Mr. Petrisch and Mr. Klein and we talked a lot about how peaceful life was settling in. That is, what I saw in 1993 is now being repaired, but in 1996, it seemed to be in the same state as if frozen, as on my first visit to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. You say the same situation. So in order to understand you correctly, so between 1995 and 1993, is that what you are saying? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, did you have the opportunity -- I withdraw that. I will rephrase the question. Do you know the people who lived in other districts in Sarajevo, that is, the areas that were not under the so-called Muslim control, how did these people live throughout the war? What suffering were they subjected to? What do you know in your capacity as a journalist and what can you tell about this to the Chamber? I am talking about other areas you knew, for instance, the area of Grbavica, Ilijas, that is the exterior -- external district that were in Serb hands --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question is compound. It contains leading elements in each aspect of it, and I hesitate to intervene because of the time situation. But the witness could have been asked whether or not he made any observations of the areas outside of the Muslim controlled part of Sarajevo, instead of tell the witness what the areas are, telling the witness about suffering, and there are a variety of leading other elements in this compound question which I object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see how is this question leading. What I was asking the witness was if he knew how the people who were in these other neighbourhoods in Sarajevo, how they suffered. And he could answer a lot or not at all. He could give any answer. So it is not a leading question. Now, it is not a leading question asking about the Serb areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It wouldn't be the first question, whether the witness has visited the areas or whether he knows anything about it. And suffering is leading to the extent that the neutral expression would be what the witness knows about the circumstances of life, since the question how there were suffering includes that they were suffering. To that extent, the question certainly is leading. There is no objection whatsoever to deal with the issues you want to raise with this question, but the questions are leading. Apart from that, there are several questions in one question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, first of all, do you know if Sarajevo was divided in several areas, but I believe you have already told that to us. Could you please answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, what could you tell us, generally speaking, about the war in relation to the other districts in Sarajevo, if, of course, you are able to tell us something about this.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I can repeat that in 1993, I visited only the Muslim part of Sarajevo. In 1995, I managed to visit the Serb part of Sarajevo. It was with the support of the Russian battalion we were there. We could see that Muslims were not only victimised by the war but the Serb side; namely, that they lived under those very difficult conditions, and also that they were killed and wounded among them and that they were also short of medicines and other things. But this was later, as I said, it was in 1995. In 1993, I repeat, we were only in the Muslim part. It was only later I could also see in what way -- what things -- how things were in the Serb part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, since you told us that they too suffered, if I understood you correctly, because of the war and this until the very end of the war, could you perhaps tell us, elaborate on this specifically. What did you see at the time, something that would be of use for later, something that you saw with your own --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The conditions that might obtain in the areas outside of those covered by the indictment might be marginally relevant, I would submit respectfully, during the indictment period. But I would submit that it becomes absolutely irrelevant when we are being asked about areas outside of the indictment period and outside of the indictment area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has expressed many times that times outside of the scope in time of the indictment may have some relevance, although perhaps less direct relevance than those events that happened within these period of times. So if the Defence would keep in mind that the relevance, of course, is a different one, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Present, I will do it, but I would like to make the observation that it seems to me that today there is a change of the indictment today, since we are talking about a territorial restriction above all and not a chronological restriction. And the Defence would like to make this observation for the formal reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, when you returned to 1995, could you tell us what time it was exactly. When did you go to Sarajevo? When was it, what season was it?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: We were there in August 1995. And after that, but at that time, it was a very difficult to get there because we were travelling by car and we travelled from Split and then escorted by an UN convoy, we crossed Mount Igman, but on Mount Igman we were all left to our own duresses --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am going to have to stop you because we don't have enough time. Thank you, but could you please tell us what were the communities that you visited, the neighbourhoods, the areas that you visited yourself?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: In 1996, we could move around freely because we were escorted by our UN representatives and we were protected by the Russian Battalion. So we could move around the whole city because we were in UN cars and our cameraman was recording everything. So we had interviews with representatives and this was a major interest in Russia because we are selling gas to Yugoslavia. So many questions: Well, why is Russia not delivering gas to Sarajevo? And that is why we decided to make a story about the work of the gas enterprise in Sarajevo. We were shown how it worked and we talked with the representative of the gas company in Sarajevo. Then we went to the Serb part of Sarajevo. We met with the leaders of the Russian Battalion --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I am sorry, I am going to have to stop you here. First of all, I asked you a question in relation to 1995. Are you talking about this period or are you speaking about a different period of time?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I am speaking about 1995. 1995 November, and that is why I remember well because on the 7th of November --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. If I have asked you that question, it is just for the purposes of transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: There is certainly an interpretation problem in 43:6, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell us, what were the areas that you visited, do you remember at that time?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: To begin with, by that time the war was coming to an end. There were negotiations at the -- Patterson base, that is, the Dayton Accords were already -- Moscow wanted to know what was going on in Sarajevo at that time. Was there a cease-fire, whether it was being complied with, and how city lived. So we got there in order to tell the Russian audiences how the city lived at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You spoke about the suffering during the war very briefly. I have another two or three very brief questions. Briefly, could you tell us how were you able to feel that? How was this demonstrated in this areas of Sarajevo? Could you please tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Well, how can a person feel himself if he comes to a city where there is there is a war going on and has been going on for quite a while? How can you talk to people who have lived through the blockade, people on both sides. It is a tragedy, naturally, it is a tragedy for all the people involved. So as far as I see it, an ordinary man, regardless of his patriotism, doesn't really care much about what is going on in the city. All he cares about is his own life.
