It perhaps sounds pathetic, but it was difficult to live through that war, and everybody had people killed in their families, a brother, a child, somebody had people die in their arms. So there were so many tragedies everywhere around. I don't want to elaborate on this, but one could feel in the air a tragedy in that town. And the impression that most struck me, especially in 1993, one could always feel in this city that there was not a normal life going on. There was something unnatural happening there. And somebody -- people could feel that somebody living on the other side were fighting them. There was an action and counteraction. I want to say that as far as the Russians are concerned, the Muslims were more neutral with respect to them than respect to Serbs. But I want to say that every time a journalist came to Sarajevo, he or she took a certain risk. We knew how our colleagues from CNN worked, how our French colleagues worked there, and we knew that cameramen were frequently targeted by snipers. We know about this. So it was very dangerous to work there at any rate always.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, just for the transcript, in line 14 and 15 of page 44, there is something missing. I believe that we are talking about a blockade here. I believe that the witness spoke each time on both sides about a blockade. I don't know whether we are able to find it or whether I should ask the question again. I think that perhaps it could be found on the audiotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could first ask the witness, did you use the word "blockade," and in what context to explain us what, because it does not appear in the transcript. And Mr. Piletta-Zanin tells us that the word "blockade" was used by you. Could you clarify how and in what context you used that expression, if you did so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did use the word "blockade." I said that my grandfather was killed during World War II. He was taking supplies to Leningrad which was under blockade and he fell under ice. So the blockade in Leningrad is something that I associate with the blockade in Sarajevo. People in those blockades lived under unnatural circumstances. They fought each other. There were shortages of everything, of food, of medical supplies, and when I say "blockade," this is something that I mean under this word, both in Leningrad and in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of the Judges has now the audio. Do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have audio on four. I am just wondering -- yes. I have audio on five as well. Could we just check whether -- yes, Judge Nieto-Navia also has audio on four. Yes. May I ask you one additional question in relation to the answer you just gave. You were talking about a blockade and that the situation in Sarajevo reminded you of a blockade. Could you explain, blocking who? Because you didn't express yourself on that. Both parties blocking each other? One party blocking another one? Could you express how you experienced that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it was a mutual blockade; Serbs fought Muslims and Muslims fought Serbs. The town was closed from all directions. I don't know whether the Serbs were able to leave the area that was under their control, just like the Muslims couldn't leave the area under their control. And the only links Sarajevo had with Split went through a tunnel. And from what I know, people went through that tunnel and would end up in Mount Igman. So the only supplies that came in came in from the Mount Igman. So it was a double-sided blockade. It was not a natural life that went on there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, very briefly, because I only have a few minutes left, I would just like to know whether you were there and I have to ask a leading question for once. Were you present during some sniping incidents in Sarajevo while you were there?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I didn't see that personally with my own eyes. But my colleagues that attended funerals of children in Sarajevo at the time saw a Turkish journalist killed at a funeral. It was said that he was killed by a sniper, and we had no confirmation as to who had done it. So there was a case of that and Irina Vogonina and Najasov Nagrasov [phoen] And another colleague of mine can confirm this. They were present at a funeral when this happened, and I heard it from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am going to have to interrupt you now. I am talking about your personal knowledge, Witness, not about what you may have heard. We all may have heard things, but you personally, were you able to see while you were in Sarajevo, were you an eyewitness to a sniping incident?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: No. I did not witness that. But I can remember now that as we were waiting to have an interview with Mr. Izetbegovic, that building was shielded from all sides by other buildings in the area. So I was there with a colleague of mine from a paper in Russia, and we wanted to take pictures of each other, and there was a part of open area there. And as we crossed that area, it seemed to me that there was a sniper shot, and that is the only thing I can tell you. That is the only thing I personally witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What was your impression of these facts? Not necessarily at that very moment, but later when you thought about it.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: My impression was that I was very lucky to get back to Moscow healthy and alive, not being wounded. And the fact that I spent some time in a city where there was a war going on and where people hated each other so much that they were ready to exterminate each other. It just gave me a feeling of very unnatural abnormal human relations among people who used to be friendly to each other in the past and then all of a sudden started fighting each other. So I had a feeling that all of that was not normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, my question was in relation to this event, to this sniping incident that you witnessed, not on the totality of your journey. Were you able to interpret this incident in a certain way? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Practically I was not. Because when we inquired who had done it, they just said "somebody shot from the hill." And it was difficult to ask any questions. If you had just recently been targeted by a sniper, then it was difficult to put any questions. All I can say is that I was very lucky at the time, and that is all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know -- Witness, do you know if there were any acts of provocation from one of the parties, specifically in relation to trips made by journalists?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Leading question. I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Mr. President, I thought that the procedure was such is that when there were things that were not contested by either party, then we would let it go in order to save time. But if this is really considered to be too much of a leading question, I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I take it that the issue was not in dispute, therefore you objected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The issue as to whether or not -- and let me try to be careful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we have to deal with it in the absence of the witness, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The issue in a general sense that something might have happened on occasion is not disputed. However, in relation to this witness who spent a week approximately in Sarajevo, to put a particular situation in his mouth, is in our submission, objectionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please rephrase your question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, were you targeted, you or your group, by other similar shots like the one that you told us about in other circumstances, that is, elsewhere, if I understand correctly, like the one a few metres from the Presidency building?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: It was only on that one occasion as we were waiting to have an interview from Izetbegovic, and apart from that, neither I nor my colleagues were targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were you accompanied by people from Sarajevo at that time and that moment, people who were escorting you, guards or officials from Sarajevo? Were there any people like that with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes. There were people escorting us. I think that there was a Minister of Information of Bosnia-Herzegovina with us. We were waiting there. And we were told that we were only allowed to stand in the shielded area, not in the open area. And, yes, there were people there who escorted us and who witnessed this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. These people that were escorting you at the time, were these people in panic, in particular panic because of the firing? Were they running to and fro at that time when you were targeted?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: There was no particular panic there. People were used by that time to that kind of firing. But it was an uncomfortable situation and we got in this incident because we were stupid enough to go into the open area. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, this calm and tranquility of your escorts, didn't it seem surprising to you after the fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase the question. We will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is not -- if you put a question to a witness which is leading and then you rephrase it, you might be aware that the leading effect is not undone. So, therefore, I told you before, if you use leading questions where they are objectionable, then you risk that additional questions will be put to the witness. Please proceed, at this very moment. The question was whether the reaction of your -- those who escorted you surprised you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was practically not surprised, and I will repeat once again, perhaps the translation was not right. People were used to that by that time, so it was not unexpected for them. And for us, it was a bit unusual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The translation was perfect. We understood you quite well. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you told us that you would need another 30 minutes. That is now approximately 50 minutes ago. So...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I forgot to tell you this was my very last question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Talking about surprises, the very last question where there is no last question or very last question indicated before not surprise this Chamber a bit -- no, let's remain serious. Mr. Stamp, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you recall what week it was, what time it was in the summer of 1993 that you went to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: It is hard to say now. I can't remember exactly. I know it was in July, but it has been nine years since. And I not only travelled to Sarajevo, I travelled all over the world, so it is hard for me to pinpoint exactly when I was there. But it was in July in 1993 when I was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall how many days you spent in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I think that it was either five days or a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many times did you visit the Kosevo Hospital complex? Do you remember if it was once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long did you spend there?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: About two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the two hours you spent, was it inside this children's ward that you described?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: No. We were not only to the children's ward, we also went to interview the chief doctor, the surgeon of that hospital who told us about how the hospital functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you interviewed the chief doctor in his office. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The time that you spent at the hospital you were in the children's ward and in the chief doctor's office. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: No, not only children's ward. We went to several wards, but let me tell you once again that it is difficult for me to remember everything exactly. What particularly impressed me were the wounded children and the children's ward. We also saw some other wards there as well, but most of the time we spent interviewing the chief doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. When you moved around Sarajevo, by what means did you travel?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: We were driven in a very old car which could be described as a mini-van, Volkswagon, or a Ford. It was a Polish-made vehicle that practically had no windows except for the window shield in front of the driver. So practically all of the windows were blocked. And we were driven very fast by a local [Realtime transcript read in error "legal"] driver who knew the area, and he was our main escort, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The five days to one week which you spent in Sarajevo, were those days spent in the Presidency side or on both sides? Did you visit the Serb side on all of those days or was it on the Presidency side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, has this question already been answered implicitly? I did hear you say that in 1993 you only could be on the Presidency side, but when you returned in 1995, you also under the escort of the Russians that you could visit the other side, was that -- is my understanding correct? Yes? You are nodding, but nodding does not appear on the transcript. Was my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am sorry, I am just going to have to interrupt, because I am not sure that I understood well, that is, I am not sure that I heard the expression "legal driver" which appears in the transcript. It seems rather surprising to me. I don't know what it could possibly mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I certainly did not hear "the legal driver" but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think he said "local driver."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is line one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My translation was "local driver."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Local driver," yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that particularly in 1993 your impression was that people could feel that there were or there was somebody living on the other side fighting them. And the question is: The people that you speak of who could feel that there was somebody on the other side fighting them, were these people the civilians that you met, the ordinary civilians in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: What I had in mind were not ordinary people. I knew that there was an army on both sides and armies fought each other and people, ordinary people, suffered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that the people were ready to exterminate each other, and that was your impression. Was it your impression that the people in Sarajevo that you met in 1993 were the victims of an attempt to exterminate them; is that what you meant? I am just quoting from what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- The Defence knows perfectly well that leading questions are possible in cross-examination but, however, such a question goes much further than it an admissible, whether the witness asked -- answered this in relation to both parties, I don't think that this question is going much too far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is not -- from a legal point of view, I would say, asking for confirmation of one part of a double answer, might as such not be impermissible. But, Mr. Stamp, you are talking about the people in Sarajevo, which is a very unprecise use of wording at this moment. Your impression that the people in Sarajevo that you met over -- that you met in 1993. May I just ask you the following question: If you say that both parties, that you had the impression that both parties were at a point, even willing to exterminate each other, that the Serbs were willing to exterminate the other party, which I would then define as the Muslims and perhaps Croats in the city of Sarajevo while the inhabitants of the city of Sarajevo were at a point of willing to exterminate the Serbs that were in control of other parts of the city? Is that what you -- what your answer was about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I had in mind. There was a war, a mutual war, on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand that there was a war. What I want to ask you is what you meant when you said what you said. Did you form the impression that the ordinary civilian person on both sides of the confrontation line felt that the other side was ready to exterminate them, and that they were being targeted by persons on the other side?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I can repeat that I was on one side only, and talked only to the inhabitants of Sarajevo in the Muslim part. And people were saying that war was being waged against them, and that they were ready to fight for themselves with the help of their army, with the assistance of weapons, to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was it your impression when you said that people could feel that there was somebody on the other side fighting against them, and people hated each other so much that they were ready to exterminate people on the other side, that particularly in 1993, the people in Sarajevo felt that they were being targeted from persons on the other side?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is the second time that Mr. Stamp asked this question. I don't think that he can ask over the same question over and over again if he has received an answer already. I am talking about the fact that people were targeted. The witness has already answered this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kacalin, there seems to be some misunderstanding perhaps on your answers, where one of the parties says that its question was clearly answered, where the other party says that, at least, suggests that it was not yet answered. Let me try and see whether I understood your answers until now, well. Was your answer that you got the impression that there was a war going on, that on both sides people would fight back -- that these people would fight until the bitter end, and that in 1993 you got this impression on the basis of your stay within the city, which would mean that you then, at least, got the impression that the citizens within the city felt being attacked by those outside the city, where perhaps later on you got similar impressions when you also visited other areas of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You understood me well. That is what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you then please proceed on another subject, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were in Sarajevo, did you become aware of allegations or statements that there was sniping of civilians within Sarajevo by persons from outside the confrontation lines? Did you hear of that while you were there?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: We were warned before we left for Sarajevo that there was sniper war in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before you went to Sarajevo or while you were in Sarajevo, you were warned about a sniper -- or my question is: While you were there, were you told that civilians within Sarajevo were being sniped by persons from outside of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Well, I was a civilian who was targeted by a sniper, whether by accident or not. But it could have happened to me, to become a victim of a sniper bullet, and I was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but may I ask you to answer precisely to the question. The question was whether you heard of other people in addition to your own experience, perhaps that there was sniping going on at civilians in the city of Sarajevo from outside the city, whether you heard that from other people, that is the question. So apart from your own experience.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Siljadzic, the mufti, they all talked about that. Each one -- everybody talked about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am not sure if I understand your answer. You named some figures of some significance and said that they talked about it, but then you continued by saying "each one, everybody talked about it." Did the journalists and the ordinary civilians in Sarajevo that you spoke to speak about it?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Including journalists and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And, of course, there were references to this sort of thing on the international news media, including CNN.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes. Journalists spoke about it, the CNN or BBC, there were a number of journalists there, representatives of the United Nations, that is, this information was corroborated by all sides by international organisations, inhabitants of Sarajevo, and the officials of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the same information in respect to sniping which you have just told us was corroborated by all sides, did you receive that same information in respect of the shelling of civilians within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in relation to the expression "by all sides," it seems to me highly ambiguous, if I understand it as I read it, or as I read it as I understand it, it means that all sides might be included, for instance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the question was referring to the answer just given. And I think that all sides is explained in that answer and could create no confusion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question was, and the same information that you received in respect of sniping and which you told us was corroborated by all sides and was even on the international press: Did you receive that same information in respect of the civilians while you were in Sarajevo in 1993?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: No, there were no such incidents during my time there. I already said that I was not there when artillery attacked the city. So it was -- there was no talk about it. But all of the western colleagues -- and I shall repeat , there was a war going on and there was fire from two sides. So it is very difficult when one side fired against the other side silently, and the other one responded loudly. I repeat, there was a war going on and there was fighting going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were in Sarajevo in 1993, did you receive any information about the shelling of civilians? Were you informed about that in Sarajevo? That is the same question I asked you before. Could you answer that question and then we will move on.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: At that time when we were there, there were no such incidents, but there was talk about it, that there were such incidents before we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you -- sorry -- did you hear of an incident of the 12th of July 1993 where civilians were killed and many wounded at a water pump in the Dobrinja area of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: There was talk about it, but I did -- that is, people talked about it, said that that had happened, that there was a story on the CNN and our colleagues spoke about it, but I did not witness it. All I saw was the TV shots of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you go to Dobrinja while you were in Sarajevo in 1993?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I don't know what is Dobrinja. Because the part of the city where we spent most of our time there, so we went to the airport through that village which was completely destroyed, and we were basically only in the central part of the city. And we didn't move anywhere further than that, because at that time the movement was pretty restricted. We couldn't just walk around the city as we pleased.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand you are saying that you did not move very much outside of the centre of the city where you stayed at. But what I want explained to me is what you mean by "restricted"? Do you mean by "restricted" that it was risky, it was dangerous to move in certain areas of the city?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Well, had we -- if we went to the hotel in an APC of the Ukrainian Battalion and from the hotel to the airport, it means it was dangerous around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said that you saw that persons were buried in the vicinity of certain streets. Can you say why there was this practice?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I didn't see people being buried in the streets. What I am saying is that we were told that there were a number of cemeteries around the city because many people are getting killed or dying. But I did not attend any funerals, so it is difficult for me to say. It wasn't on the street exactly. It was former boulevards and near the stadium. But Muslims kept saying that there were many people dying or being killed in the city, and that is why there were many cemeteries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have no further questions. May it please you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your leave, perhaps it is necessary to ask once again two or three questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends. You are allowed to ask questions on issues that came up during the cross-examination. In general terms, as you know, there is no opportunity to re-open the examination-in-chief. So if you would tell us what the subject is and how it would relate to the cross-examination, then we could consider whether your request can be granted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is not switched on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] Your microphone is not working.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know whether it is working. It should work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that it is lit, but it should work. But nevertheless, did the interpreters now hear the voice of Mr. Piletta-Zanin? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have three questions, Mr. President, and they seem to arise from the cross-examination. The first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said that you had seen the television coverage of the incident which happened on the 12th of July 1993, that is, shelling of individuals queueing for water. Can you tell us, what was it that was recorded? For instance, was it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you are in chief. At this very moment, you are giving -- you are starting to give a few opportunities. Could you just ask the witness what he has seen on this -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes. Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you saw on television?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: The CNN story said that people queueing for water were shelled by -- that is, that they were caught in the fire and were killed. So what we saw not that the moment of shelling, but people who had got killed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. because a shot had been fired from a mortar. So that was the story which was shown on the American channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Talking about -- since we are talking about killed people, did you see anybody else except killed people?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I don't remember all the nuances, but I remember that the principle story was that people who were in the water queue, because there was a shortage of water there, had gotten killed. The story was done -- it was very characteristic of American television. The event and the commentaries, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you about sources of information and quoted CNN and BBC. What were your impressions about these sources of information, that is, what did you think of the media during the war?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Well, since there were no other sources of information, only western journalists were working in Sarajevo, so therefore the information was only about what was happening in the city as they saw it. And I know that a Greek colleague of mine worked of a long time in Sarajevo; he also received several awards for this. People -- people worked there and showed what was going on in Sarajevo. And their colleague whose worked on the Serb side was showing what was happening on this side. That is what I know. Other sources of information, that is Russian journalists, or rather we had no journalists from Russia who would be working for any of our television stations. Christiane Amanipour who was CNN's correspondent in Sarajevo and stayed there for quite a long time and journalists who were -- who worked in the Serb part of Sarajevo, those were Vladimir Solovjov with a cameraman, but they used to travel to the Serb part of Sarajevo from Belgrade. And they showed the developments on the Serb side of Sarajevo, and western journalists were providing information only from the Bosnian side of Sarajevo. And we came for the programme Vlame to show how things were inside the -- inside Sarajevo itself, but that was in 1995, that I went to make some footage for that programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You used a moment ago the term "to exterminate." I think that you then explained very clearly what you meant. Do you know perhaps one symbolic object, whichever, in Sarajevo -- I am talking about buildings in the first place -- which could have been the object of destruction of such destruction that would justify the term "extermination"? I mean, are there building of cultural or something -- yes or no -- I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what the objection would have been of Mr. Stamp, but I may draw your attention to the fact that the words "to exterminate" has been used in examination-in-chief first, and then the other part of your question had got hardly got anything to do with the cross-examination on this specific word. But since you have withdrawn that question, it is not relevant anymore. Since the Judges have not just one but a few questions to you, I think it is wiser to have the break now. So these questions of the Judges will be put to you after the break, it will not take very long. We will adjourn until five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kacalin, Judge Nieto-Navia has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You told us that when you arrived to Sarajevo you were moved from the airport to the hotel by the Ukrainian soldiers, I think, using an APC. My question is whether that APC had windows, were those windows big or small, and whether you could easily see the city?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Russian APC is a large vehicle and our entire group was able to fit in there. So we were able to see through the little firing windows. And on one occasion, they even opened a door and we were able to see through this door. It was a moment when we were passing through a safe area. So we did have quite an ample opportunity to see through, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: That is all the questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi also has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Sir, if I understand you correctly, your visit to Sarajevo from 1993, the very first time you visited, that visit was about the city of Sarajevo. And during your testimony you told us something about a city that was completely destroyed. You told us about the village that was completely destroyed. If I understand you correctly, that was a neighbourhood or was that an area in the city or was that a village next to the city that you had the opportunity to visit? I am talking about page 60 of the transcript. I am going to quote you in English [In English] "completely destroyed." [Interpretation] Could you perhaps elaborate on this, thank you.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain. When we drove in that Ukrainian APC, then we saw near the airport the neighbourhood of Sarajevo or a suburb of Sarajevo where the houses were practically destroyed. They had no roofs. Some homes were completely ruined and some were seriously damaged. And then I also said that the building of Oslobodjenje newspaper was also destroyed. I saw that the window panes on the Unis building were broken, and also Unis buildings were not destroyed but burnt down. These are -- these are the examples of the destruction that I saw. I also mentioned the Europa hotel that was also destroyed. So this road from the airport to Sarajevo -- I don't know exactly what that area is called, this is what I saw -- and also certain buildings in Sarajevo that were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. So when you say "village," what you meant, you meant a neighbourhood, an area in the city, of the city?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. Because that was a part of Sarajevo, a part that was -- the part that was close to the Butmir airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Another question, please: You spoke of injured children that you saw at a hospital during your visit to the hospital. Do you know how were they injured, by whom, in what circumstances, and what were their ages, approximately, and their number? Could you perhaps tell us more about this, please.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I said that there were children up to age 10 there, and there were different injuries. We were told that they were injured in the course of fighting and shelling, and that shells landed in children's play areas. And I saw children without arms children with abdominal wounds. They were serious wounds that I saw, and these are the children that were shown to us. Now, as to where exactly those children had been wounded, we didn't really know. It was enough for us to see these wounded children to get a very tragic picture of what was happening in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what about their number? Could you tell us more about that? How many were there?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I don't know how many children were in that ward. Seven, eight, nine. I can't tell you exactly, but there was a significant number of them and the children had wounds that were serious enough to produce a tragic impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You also said that the surgeon of the hospital who welcomed you, that this woman had also been injured herself. Did this surgeon tell you, was this person injured during the work at the hospital or outside of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: First of all -- first of all, it was a man, not a woman, a man of some 45 to 50 years who told me how he had been -- he did not tell he how he has been wounded, he simply told me that he had recently just come back to work and then he told me about his work and about the operation of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My very last question, I apologise, but this is about something that you said during your testimony speaking -- and I am going to quote you -- you said: "That the city was suffering particularly in 1993." And if I understand you correctly, it was 1993, and you only visited the part of the city that was under the control of the Presidency forces. So what you are saying is that the city that you described as a suffering city, that was the city under the control of the Presidency, not the other area, the area under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I stayed in the Muslim part of Sarajevo, but as far as I know, when we travelled from the airport to our hotel, as I was later told, that was a Serb area. So the destruction that took place did not occur in 1993 when we were there, but earlier in 1992. This is what I heard from my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So, just to check something. When you say that the city was suffering, what you mean to say is that the city that you saw or at least the part of the city that you saw which was under the control or under the Serb authority or the city "lato sensu," the city -- the entire city, because you spoke of 1993?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: In the wider sense of the word, on both sides this was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kacalin, I have two questions for you, both concerning the hospital. You have described the hospital, including the children's ward, as functioning relatively normal. You also described the wounded children. You do not know exactly the number, but could you give us an impression on what was the percentage of patients in the children's ward that was treated for wounding, visible being wounded, and what percentage for, I would say, illnesses that would not show any wounds to a visitor?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: They show us only the ward for the wounded children. And as to how many other patients there were there, we were not told that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am just asking about those wards that you saw. It might have been totally different than other wards. But what was approximately the percentage of those treated for visible wounds and compared to patients not showing, at least not that you could see, any wounds?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: They showed us the wards for the most seriously wounded, the most difficult traumas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly if your answer is that the ward you saw was exclusively treating wounded people rather than ordinary sick patients?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: It was a ward only for wounded children. They showed this to us in order to depict that there were many seriously wounded children there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Next question about any damage on the roof. You said you didn't notice any, but it was not your first -- the first thing you would look at when visiting a hospital. Do you remember whether these were settled roofs or flat roofs?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: Those were contemporary modern buildings and they had flat roofs. There were no ceramic tile roofs there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would that mean that if you would be at ground level, that if there would have been damage on the roofs, you might not have seen it because the roofs were flat? If you would have paid attention to it, of course.

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: We didn't pay attention to that but I will repeat, because I am now remembering this, and it is most likely that the roof in the hospital was not destroyed. The hospital operated normally, as usual, and it treated wounded and sick children and adults.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers. Mr. Kacalin -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will give us your authorisation, Mr. President, there is just one more question stemming from one of your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will ask you to repeat -- yes, yes, thank you. Witness, a question asked by Judge El Mahdi, you said that you went next or through a Serb area from the airport, going from the airport. Now, my question is the following, and it is a two-part question: Firstly, this Serb area, did it contain considerable devastation which is what I understood that you said; and secondly, was this the part of town known as Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: KONSTANTIN KACALIN
utterances.text: I will repeat that on the left side, as one is riding from the airport, there was a village there first. And as I later learned from Ukrainian officers, that was a Serb area. And there was serious destruction there. The homes there were one- and two-storey. I will repeat, we went through that part of the town, but I don't know what it is called. Even now, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kacalin, this concludes your testimony in this court. I know it is a long way to come to The Hague. I thank you very much for coming and answering the questions of both parties and the Judges. And I wish you a safe trip home again. Mr. Usher --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom, and may I, at the same time, whether they are ready to call their next witness. Yes. Mr. Usher, could you bring the next witness as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you are Dr. Lazic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And the text of this declaration will be handed out to you now, by the usher. May I had invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Lazic. Please be seated. You will first be examined by counsel for the Defence. Is it you, Ms. Pilipovic, or Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow it, Mr. President, first of all, your humble servant, myself, and Ms. Pilipovic, since we have to work differently. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I would be very grateful, as much as you can, to answer briefly, if you can, yes or no answers, if that is possible. Witness, what is your professional qualification, very briefly, in a nutshell?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC
utterances.text: I am a surgeon. I am working at the clinical centre at the clinical hospital in Nis. I am the head of the trauma department. My title is that of professor. I specialised in surgery in 1976. I believe that is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that you are currently working in Nis. Could you tell us, before Nis what were various locations where you worked?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I see that on the transcript at 76, I finished in 1986, 86.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC
utterances.text: I finished the faculty in Nis, and the specialisation. I have been working all the time except for it time I worked in Sarajevo as a surgeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please specify what is this period of time when you worked in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC
utterances.text: I worked in Sarajevo from the 1st of November, 1992, until the 1st of February, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us what made you decide to go and work in Sarajevo? Could you tell us why? Why and how?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC
utterances.text: Because in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Sarajevo, there was a war that was being waged, and I watched on TV and read in the papers. There were many casualties. And the media said that there were not enough surgeons there, so as a doctor and humanitarian, that goes without saying, I wanted to go down there and help the people who, at the end of the 20th century, were dying because there were not enough surgeons, and they were dying from bleeding. Also, the ministry of health of Republic of Serbia called upon all the surgeons, anesthesiologists, and doctors of other specialisations who would help people in the war as doctors to do their job. So I applied as a volunteer, and I went to Sarajevo. Sometime in mid-October I arrived in Pale. And from there on I went to the part of Sarajevo, which, at the time, was under the control of the Serb force where there were no hospital and there was no surgeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you used the term "volunteer." What was your status? Could you please specify that. What I mean, is your administrative status. Were you, for instance, a volunteer, civilian volunteer, or were you a military volunteer?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC
utterances.text: I was a civilian volunteer. I worked in the hospital in Ilidza. I was not paid to do this. So it was purely as a volunteer and a humanitarian. I worked as a surgeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about Sarajevo and about Ilidza. Could you tell the Chamber if you visited other areas, apart from the Ilidza neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC
utterances.text: The hospital that was located in the municipality of Ilidza covered five Sarajevo municipalities, Vogosca, Ilijas, Rajlovac, Hadzici, Ilidza and the settlement of Nedzarici. There at the time, there were about 100 thousand people living there. And the only hospital at that time and for the next year, perhaps less, I was the only general surgeon, the only surgeon who was able to do surgeries of chest, stomach, and internal organs. I visited all these municipalities for the duration of the three and a half years during my stay in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you have an opportunity to also visit the Grbavica area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC
utterances.text: I was in Grbavica only once, sometime at the end of 1995, after the Dayton Agreement was signed, perhaps 10, 15 days later, before that, I was not able to go to Grbavica, nor to the Sarajevo municipality surrounding Grbavica under the control of the Serb forces, because it was impossible, because the road went -- going through the airport was closed to passage and if you went the round about way, it would take eight to ten Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. hours, and it was a very dangerous road. I had no reason to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, can you tell us what kind of surgical interventions did you perform in your hospital during -- at the time that you volunteered there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC
utterances.text: I did both war surgery and peacetime surgery, that is, as for the former, all types of injuries of the chest, abdomen, and vascular injuries. All types of injuries sustained at time of war. At the same time, I also operated on the inhabitants who suffered from peacetime complaints, which can happen at any time, such as appendicitis or ulcers or similar complaints because there was no other hospital which could treat patients suffering of peacetime complaints.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you were a civilian volunteer, did you -- your patients, did they belong to one category or another category? What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC
utterances.text: We had military patients and civilian patients, that is anybody who has sustained injuries in that part of the city came to us, that is, military and civilians, and I mean children, and women, and elderly, and men, and soldiers, adults, that is all the categories of people who lived in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And finally, to make it more precise, Doctor, you made a distinction between the civilian medicine in a way and war medicine?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC
utterances.text: Yes, because of wartime surgery is pretty specific because there are injuries inflicted with different weapons and tools so that this is a specific area of surgery. And, of course, it depends on the type of the weapon on the incidents of injuries, and, of course, whether they are inflicted by heavy weaponry, what type of instruments, and so on and so forth. And you also have, for instance, heavy artillery was used and we have also called poly-tramatised, patients -- that is patients with multiple injuries who are very difficult to treat and which are also highly painful to those involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Right. You tell us about artillery and other shots. But when you speak about war surgery, wartime surgery, was it restricted to this or that type of patients?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC
utterances.text: Well, injuries caused by different types of weapons and tools, they did not -- they were not choosing terms of either sex or age, because the area was densely populated. Military and civilians were mixed. So that a possible case of shelling or sniping would cause injuries among both categories, from children to other civilians, to the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Doctor, can you tell us, if you know, what was the share of the wounded in your hospital, the share of those who were strictly military, and other wounded individuals? For instance, jeba [phoen] year to see if there was any revolution of a time, if there was any?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC
utterances.text: What I can say, since I was there between 1995 and 2002 and I wrote a number of papers on war surgery for our local and international Congresses, so I have information between 1995 and 1995, 8.723 [Realtime transcript read in error "1.723"] patients passed through the hospital. About 68 [Realtime transcript read in error "60] per cent were military wounded, and about 32 per cent were civilian wounded. Of that -- of the latter figure about 470 were wounded children, and children are up to 14 years of age which means that everything fifth wounded civilian was a child. On the average, it means that we had several wounded per day, but this is only the main figure. At times we had one or two; at times we had several dozen. Be that as it may, hardly a day passed without a wounded and an injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For technical reasons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just intervene, could the witness please repeat the general number of -- as I understood from the French translation -- wounded and where the transcript says "1.723," is that the correct number? That is the correct number. These were wounded as I understood from the French translation? Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can we clarify it -- yes, please, go on.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC
utterances.text: I see that the number of wounded was 8.123 -- 8.123 wounded. This does not include people suffering from peacetime complaints. But 68 [Realtime transcript read in error "60"] per cent were military and 32 per cent were civilians. So there is a mistake. 60 and 1.700, which means seven wounded per day which does not mean we had seven patients every day. At times there were less and at times there were more. So I am talking only about the wounded. I am not talking about patients suffering from other kind of complaints.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel's microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: To clarify matters, Doctor, the transcript, I see that it was 68 per cent of the military and 32 per cent of the civilians, then, if I am able to add this up, it makes 92, and what about the rest or is there a mistake?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I do not know how your system works but 68 plus 32, in my view, is 100. Your question is that you are missing some, but I have some 100 per cent. It has been in the second round been adjusted. That it was 68 per cent. I do agree with you in the first round it was 60 and 32, but then -- yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am afraid we are not getting any translation at this part here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there is no translation of your question. Would you please repeat your question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I shall be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The question was: You also mentioned children. What can you tell us about children whom you treated during your stay in Sarajevo, in general terms?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC
utterances.text: I have just said that in accordance with the medical classification, children up to 14 years of age. I also said that there were about 470 injured children, either by infantry weapons or by artillery weapons. So children were major victims. Every fifth wounded civilian was a child. And you can find it all in my paper I presented in Sarajevo late last year at the international conference on the suffering of children which was the organised, I believe it was under the auspices of this Tribunal with the sponsorship of the Dutch government. And at this two-day gathering in Sarajevo, more than 100 papers was represented and I was one of the orders. And I spoke about the suffering of those children. So I can say they were wounded by both type of fire weapons. That they were children who were wounded mostly in urban areas, and I think the reason for it, that children as a category were most frequently in the streets. And the shells which hit the asphalt ricochetted in all directions, that is the reason there were so many wounded children in all five Sarajevo municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Doctor, how do you know explain the number of wounded due to what you called "artillery weapons" that is, if I understand you well shelling?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG LAZIC
utterances.text: Every doctor can't distinguish by a wound inflicted by infantry weapons and artillery weapons. That is, to make a difference by wounds caused by different explosions, caused by major artillery weapons and small arms. Doctors with wartime experience can also tell apart wounds inflicted by artillery weapons and also can identify weapons inflicted on such wounds on the basis of a major experience and a larger number of the wounded, one can tell apart artillery weapons from small arms and the wounds inflicted by small weapons are highly mutilating.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I cannot hear the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Will you, please, try to listen carefully to my questions and my question is as follows: How does one explain the number of those children wounded by weapons which you call "artillery weapons"? How does one explain that high -- that large number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Formally, matters put on record, the objection to this whole line of questioning. I was trying to be patient. But my friend is asking questions about what appears to be incidents or persons who were injured outside of the area that we are concerned about in this trial. I think the point has already been made in respect to the relevance of this apparent tu quoque of the issues before the Trial Chamber. And secondly, I, on the basis of the evidence so far, I can see no foundation for the doctor attempting to explain why there are wounded from artillery or other types of weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I asked the questions about Sarajevo. If this is not about Sarajevo, let us then erase forever from the indictment and General Galic can go home tomorrow. Sarajevo. These are doctors who work in Sarajevo. You tell me that this is not the subject of the indictment. Well we will change it and let's go home, all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from suggesting whether we should go home or not, I think the main reason why Mr. Stamp raised the issue was the tu quoque aspect of it. Could you please respond to that briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. Absolutely not. That is not how I initialed Mr. Stamp, but we are not raising and we shall not raise the tu quoque principle. What we are trying to say, and hence the question, how can it be that this doctor knew so many children who had been wounded by shrapnel of shells? There may be some technical reason. And men who belongs to the trade who is a doctor perhaps can explain it to me. Perhaps -- and I am quite ready to accept -- I do not see how one can raise a question of tu quoque. It was -- nothing could be further from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may just add one thing briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The main thrust of the objections is that the whole line of questions about these type of casualties from these areas which are outside the areas which we claim is relevant to the indictment. But I would also invite the court to have a look at the -- well, I am not sure if the Court received a summary from the Defence in respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We have not received the summary you have got in your hands at this very moment. We have the very, very brief summary, and the Chamber invited the Defence to provide more detailed summaries to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I will not spend much time except to say that these types of casualties, if it happened, and we are not denying that there were casualties on that side, but further in the summary it is said that this witness will also state that patients of Croat ethnicity from middle Bosnia, Kisilak, Fojnica and other places were also treated in hospital. It is submitted that the testimony is irrelevant. One can take the counsel to go on for a time, but how far are we going to get into this? I don't think we should go too far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that at least, if we are talking about the numbers just mentioned, that is 32 per cent of the wounded patients being civilians, 470 children, is that contested by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is not without -- within our state of knowledge, to be able to contest or not contest. It is not -- it is submitted not relevant, especially having regard to the fact that we don't know where these children are from. The summary seems to indicate that these children could have come from any part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, your summary indicates that the patients came also from areas that were further away from Sarajevo, does your summary indicate this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear it because I am not wearing the headset, and my computer refuses to go any further -- oh, sorry. No. Obviously, Mr. President, we are not saying that there were patients. Perhaps it was the case. But we are not indicating that there were patients coming from elsewhere, except the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, I would like to see the summary. I think the Chamber would like to see the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally handed over the summary, and Mr. Stamp did not say that. And I would really appreciate it if he could say, and I would like to know why doesn't Mr. Stamp say he was disclosed this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am not contesting whether this document was disclosed or not. I had it, so it is handed over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The procedural issue at stake at this very moment is that Mr. Stamp objects against certain questions since the summary indicates that it might deal with patients coming from areas at a distance from Sarajevo. That is what Mr. Stamp claims. I asked the Defence whether this was part of the summary. The Defence said it was not. So since the parties do disagree on what is in the summary, the Chamber would like to see the summary, and whether it is given by Mr. Stamp, or by you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I take it that that is the same document. So, therefore, we would like to see the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let Mr. Stamp produce both these documents, not only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are two summaries, the Chamber would like to receive two summaries. Is there an old one and a new one or what -- how do I have to understand this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I added information today and I faxed it to the Prosecution

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you would say is that there was a previous one and this is in additional to the previous one?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, do you have the previous one for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just indicate that the first one was the one that was submitted with the 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. I haven't got it in front of me at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And there is a second one which is not very different from the first. I have the second one here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is not quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are just taking one second to read, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Lazic, there is some confusion, and let's just try to see whether we can get some clarification from you. You have been talking about wounded patients. You have not given any further details as where they would have come from. Could you describe to us from where they would have come.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you mean children --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I am talking general. First of all, Kiseljak and Fojnica, at what distance is this from the city of Sarajevo? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fojnica. So let me answer this -- or should I answer your first question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should we first do the distances and then where the patients came from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kiseljak, yes -- well I cannot be precise 100 per cent before the war and during the war it was in Sarajevo municipality, I am not sure whether it is still one, but it is about 10 kilometres away from Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten kilometers away from Ilidza in -- yes, approximately -- Fojnica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fojnica, I don't know, I didn't -- it is beyond Kiseljak, but I don't know how far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you then please answer my first question. What was the area your patients might have come from or from what places? Can you clarify this? I am talking about patients in general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said that we had 8.123 wounded, I meant Sarajevo municipalities controlled by Serb forces. Ilidza, Ilijas, Rajlovac, Ilidza, Vogosca, Rajlovac, Hadzici, and the locality of Nedzarici. To this, one should add, about 150 to 170 -- I can't give you the exact figure -- of the wounded from parts of Kiseljak and some other parts controlled by Croat forces who came to our hospital because that was the only hospital. So this figure of 8.123, about 150 to 170 were wounded from those Croat areas and who came to our hospital because they didn't have a hospital of their own. As for the children, that figure is accurate because I gave it, four children wounded in Sarajevo. So 470 children from these municipalities, not the Croat municipalities. So exclusively the five municipalities covered by the hospital. I took out -- I took out that figure for the conference in Sarajevo because that conference was on Sarajevo. So with the exception of these five municipalities, we also treated wounded from several Croat municipalities, that is, 150 to 170 Croat wounded. I can give you the names of those municipalities, if they -- if it is important to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the matter raised has been clarified. I think we can return the documents to the parties. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Know that it is the time and we shall resume tomorrow. But could the -- actually confirm that this whole line of objections concerning questions that we were asking about Sarajevo, the Greater Sarajevo, is rejected so that we don't have to come back to the same problem. So if the question concerns five municipalities around Sarajevo, and I would like to Chamber to tell us whether this line of objections is accepted or is it sustained or is it not sustained?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will give you an answer to that question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin tomorrow morning at 9.00, and that will be in Courtroom II, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Lazic, it is already past 7.00. We will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00, not in this courtroom, but in a different courtroom. But they will help you to find your way to that courtroom. We will adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.text: Before we do, is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
